title: Dynamic Hydroclimate Fuels Cryptic Sulfur Cycling and Iron and Carbon Impacts in Wetlands
content:
Abstract

Wetland water quality plays a vital role in controlling emissions of methane, a strong greenhouse gas, and it is regulated by the sequestration of nutrients and toxic metals on iron-rich soils. However, the stability of these functions under shifting precipitation and temperature regimes remains unknown, because of complex and unconstrained mechanisms through which climate and hydrology drive coupled biogeochemical processes. In particular, although increasing molecular-scale evidence suggests that “cryptic” sulfur cycling can influence carbon and iron cycles in freshwater wetland porewaters, how these interactions scale up under dynamic hydrological conditions to influence atmospheric feedbacks and water quality have been unexplored. Barriers include uncertainties in reaction rates and networks involving intermediate-valence sulfur forms, especially under variable hydrological conditions. Here we present a predictive, interdisciplinary framework that quantifies coupled iron-sulfur-carbon cycling under dynamic hyporheic flows by integrating reactive transport modeling, metagenomic sequencing, and multi-scale geochemical analyses at a riparian wetland. Simulations show that even at low sulfate concentrations, cryptic sulfur cycling enhances dissolved iron concentrations by threefold, promoting iron flocs that improve water quality, and it suppresses methane production by 26%, tempering methane emissions. Moreover, incorporating weather-driven water flux reversals on daily to seasonal scales further amplifies these effects, promoting an additional 25% in iron(II) accumulation and 20% in methane attenuation in porewater. By mechanistically linking microbial metabolism and hyporheic flow fluctuations with redox dynamics and methane production, our work demonstrates the need to consider hydrologically driven sulfur interactions, when predicting atmospheric feedbacks and contaminant dynamics in wetlands under changing climate.
